strengths: Addresses an under-explored aspect of ML-for-MILP: guaranteeing full solution feasibility without delegating to a traditional solver, and explicitly targeting non-binary integer variables rather than only binary ones.

The two-phase reward design (pre- and post-first-feasible-solution) is a sensible way to separate the feasibility-seeking objective from the optimality-improving objective, and the paper provides a clear intuitive explanation (Fig. 5) for the reward shaping choices.

The hybrid MPNN + Transformer-encoder architecture is reasonably motivated by the oversmoothing/long-range dependency issue in bipartite MILP graphs, and the paper backs the design with an ablation study (PE, phase token, separated layers) showing each component contributes to feasibility and solution quality.
The paper is generally clearly written and well organized, with helpful running examples and figures illustrating the RL loop, graph representation, and search procedure.
weaknesses: Experiments are limited to tiny, synthetically generated instances (9 and 100 variables) that Gurobi solves to optimality/near-optimality in under a second; the practical significance and scalability of the method to realistic MILP sizes (thousands+ variables) is not demonstrated or discussed quantitatively.

The empirical comparison lacks any external ML baseline: the only competitors are internal architecture ablations (MLP/CNN encoder swaps) and Gurobi itself. Despite explicitly discussing closely related prior work (Qi, Wang, and Shen 2021's RL-based feasibility pump, Han et al. 2023's predict-and-search, Nair et al. 2020's binary-encoding approach) in the related work section, none of these are empirically compared, making it hard to judge the actual advance over prior ML-based approaches.

On the larger dataset the proposed method is both slower and yields a worse RP_Gap than Gurobi (1.33% vs 0.01%), and the motivation for using this heavier, more complex learned solver instead of a mature commercial solver on such small problems is not convincingly established beyond an 'initial study' framing.

The method actually solves a restricted problem (pure integer programming with all-integer variables, and bounds fixed to [0, ∞)) rather than the general MILP setting suggested by the title and framing, which is a substantial scope limitation not fully reflected in the claims.

The reward function and search procedure involve numerous heuristic design choices and hyperparameters (interval-based rewards, local region size Δ, termination heuristics, no-change penalty of −10, scaling of f_t) without sensitivity analysis, raising concerns about robustness and the amount of tuning required to reproduce results.

No code or dataset release is mentioned, and several implementation details (network sizes, hyperparameters, training time/compute, number of Transformer layers N, GCN layers L) are not fully specified, limiting reproducibility.

The local search strategy has no optimality guarantees (acknowledged by the authors), and the paper does not provide any theoretical or empirical characterization of how far solutions can be from optimal as problem size or difficulty grows beyond the two tested instance sizes.

strengths: The paper identifies a genuine and relevant limitation of existing ML-based primal heuristics: they typically ignore feasibility guarantees and focus on binary variables, while many real applications require integer variables.
The two-phase reward design (before/after first feasible solution) is a reasonable and somewhat novel way to shape RL exploration towards feasibility first, then optimality.

The architectural ablation study (Table 3) is informative about the necessity of periodic embedding, phase tokens, and separated actor/critic layers, and shows interesting failure modes (e.g., complete infeasibility without phase tokens).

The paper is generally clearly written and the methodology (bipartite graph representation, MPNN+Transformer hybrid) is explained in adequate technical detail for reproducibility of the architecture itself.
weaknesses: Extremely limited experimental scale: only two synthetic datasets with at most 100 variables and 50 constraints, generated from a narrow random distribution (Qi et al. 2021 style). This is orders of magnitude smaller than real-world or standard MILP benchmarks (e.g., MIPLIB), making claims of practical significance for 'solving MILP end-to-end' unsupported.

The central comparison against Gurobi is not meaningful: Gurobi solves all instances to exact optimality in under 1 second at this scale, while the proposed RL method still has non-trivial optimality gaps (1.33-1.96%) and presumably far higher training cost; the paper never reports wall-clock training time or a matched-time-budget comparison that would justify the approach's value proposition over simply calling a traditional solver.

No comparison to the actual ML-based primal heuristic baselines that motivate the work (Gasse et al. 2019; Nair et al. 2020; Han et al. 2023; Cantürk et al. 2024). Instead, the only baselines are ad hoc architecture variants (M_MLP, M_CNN) created by the authors themselves, which is insufficient to substantiate the claimed advantages over prior ML-based approaches on feasibility or solution quality.

The 'end-to-end, no traditional solver' framing is undermined by the method's reliance on an LP-relaxation solve (via a traditional solver) to obtain the initial solution x0 and lower bound obj_r, which is a significant, unacknowledged dependency on classical solvers.

The problem setting is restricted to pure integer programs (all variables integer, no continuous variables, no binary variables), which is a narrow special case; despite the title and framing around 'Mixed-Integer Linear Programming,' the paper does not address the mixed-integer setting at all, and the authors do not empirically demonstrate how the approach would extend to genuinely mixed problems.

Scalability of the action formulation (per-variable increase/decrease/retain decisions with fixed magnitude 1) is a concern for larger, more realistic instances with variables spanning large ranges (as the paper itself notes in the introduction when critiquing binary-encoding approaches), yet no experiments probe this scaling behavior beyond n=100.

No variance/statistical reporting across multiple seeds or runs; single-run point estimates are reported for RP_Gap, FR, and FFST, making it hard to assess robustness of the reported improvements over M_MLP/M_CNN.

Several reward-function hyperparameters (phase-switch penalty of -10, interval-based reward shaping in phase 2, action magnitude of 1) appear to be heuristically chosen without sensitivity analysis or principled justification, raising concerns about generalizability to different MILP distributions.

Generalization is only tested within the same synthetic distribution used for training; there is no evaluation of transfer to differently structured or distributed instances, which is important given the paper's motivating claim about learning 'repetitive patterns' in MILP families.

strengths: Addresses an underexplored and legitimate gap in ML-for-MILP research: existing ML-based primal heuristics mostly focus on binary variables and delegate feasibility restoration to a traditional solver, whereas this paper attempts to produce complete feasible solutions end-to-end via RL for integer-only MILPs.

The two-phase reward design (finding first feasibility vs. improving objective while staying within an [obj_r, obj_b] interval) is a sensible and reasonably well-motivated mechanism, illustrated clearly with Figure 5.

The architectural choice of combining an MPNN-based bipartite GCN (local structure) with a Transformer encoder (global attention across variables) is well justified by the oversmoothing/long-range dependency argument (e.g., the x2-a1-x1-a2-x3 example).

The ablation study (Table 3) is informative and shows that each proposed component (Periodic Embedding, Phase Token, Separated Layers) is functionally necessary — several ablations collapse to 0% feasible rate, providing reasonably convincing evidence for design choices.
The paper is generally clearly written, with good use of figures/diagrams to explain the RL loop, graph representation, and architecture.
weaknesses: The empirical evaluation is very limited in scale: the two datasets (9 variables/18 constraints and 100 variables/50 constraints) are toy-sized for MILP, and Gurobi solves them essentially instantly (<1s, near-zero gap), which undercuts the significance of claiming 'near-optimal' results relative to a solver that is not meaningfully stressed at this scale. There is no experiment showing the method scales to problems where traditional solvers actually struggle, which is where an ML-based end-to-end solver would need to demonstrate value.

Despite extensively citing directly relevant prior work (Gasse et al. 2019, Nair et al. 2020, Han et al. 2023, Cantürk et al. 2024, and especially Qi, Wang, and Shen 2021 whose instance-generation scheme this paper reuses), the paper does not empirically compare against any of these methods. The only baselines are self-constructed ablation variants (MLP/CNN in place of the Transformer) and Gurobi, which is a much weaker basis for establishing significance than comparing to the actual competing ML approaches in the literature.

The method is restricted to the special case where all decision variables are non-binary integers (no continuous or binary variables), which is explicitly acknowledged as future work but substantially narrows applicability and makes claims about 'solving MILP end-to-end' overreaching relative to what is actually demonstrated.

The local search strategy (Algorithm 1) explicitly cannot guarantee global optimality, and no analysis is given of how performance degrades or scales with increasing problem size beyond two data points (9x18 and 100x50), leaving open how the RP_Gap trends as instances grow larger — an important question for assessing real-world usefulness.

Training appears to require fresh instance-by-instance interaction (with per-instance termination conditions) and a fairly large number of parameter updates (5,000 for the larger dataset); the paper does not report or discuss the wall-clock training cost or sample efficiency, which is relevant for judging practicality relative to traditional solvers that require no training at all.
The claim of learning 'without labeled data' as an advantage over supervised approaches is not empirically substantiated by any cost/efficiency comparison against the supervised methods it critiques.

Testing uses only 100 pre-generated instances per dataset from a single synthetic random distribution (matching training distribution), so out-of-distribution generalization and robustness to different constraint structures/densities are untested.

strengths: Addresses an underexplored aspect of ML-for-MILP: handling non-binary integer decision variables end-to-end, rather than only binary variables as in most prior ML-based primal heuristics.

The overall system design is thorough: a two-phase reward function (feasibility-seeking phase1, objective-improving phase2) grounded in a simple but clear theoretical proposition (Proposition 1) relating better solutions to the LP-relaxation bound and current incumbent.

Reasonably extensive ablations (Table 3) and sensitivity analysis over the toward-optimal bias parameter β and neighborhood/action magnitude (Table 2), which help clarify which architectural and search-strategy choices matter.
Good reproducibility support: detailed pseudocode (Algorithms 1-2), full hyperparameter/dataset-generation details in the appendix, and named baseline implementations with sources.

The proposed Transformer+MPNN hybrid architecture is a sensible response to the oversmoothing/long-range dependency issue in bipartite MILP graphs, and the ablation (Table 3) shows both components contribute.
weaknesses: Experimental scale is very small and synthetic: the largest instance (D300x100) has only 300 variables and 100 constraints, orders of magnitude smaller than realistic industrial MILPs (which can have thousands to millions of variables). This severely limits the significance of the claimed contribution as a 'full end-to-end MILP solver' capable of replacing traditional solvers.

On every tested dataset, Gurobi already solves instances to near-exact optimality in well under 1 second, while the proposed RL-MILP solver needs up to 100 seconds and still only achieves ~0.3-0.6% gap on larger instances. The paper does not demonstrate any regime (e.g., very large or structurally hard instances) where the RL approach is actually competitive with or superior to standard solvers, undermining the practical motivation.

No comparison against stronger existing learning-based baselines (e.g., predict-and-search style methods such as Han et al. 2023, or Nair et al. 2020's binary-encoding approach for integers) beyond an ablation-style MLP/CNN variant of the authors' own architecture; the paper's claim of outperforming 'existing methods' is not empirically substantiated against the actual SOTA ML-for-MILP baselines cited in the introduction.

Scalability of the action/observation space with problem size is not analyzed — the agent selects an action per variable at every timestep, and the collapse of M_CNN's feasible rate to 0% at 100+ variables raises concerns about whether the underlying RL formulation itself (not just the chosen backbone) will scale to realistic problem sizes.

Each model appears to require training tailored to a specific instance distribution/size (per-dataset training), and no experiments test generalization to unseen distributions, larger instances than trained on, or different problem structures (e.g., real-world MILPLib benchmarks), limiting evidence of general applicability.

Proposition 1, while correctly proven, is a fairly straightforward consequence of standard LP-relaxation bounding arguments already well known in the MILP literature (e.g., branch-and-bound theory), so its framing as a core theoretical contribution somewhat overstates its novelty.

The paper only evaluates on all-integer MILPs (no continuous variables), despite motivating the work with general 'mixed'-integer applications; it is unclear how the method would handle genuinely mixed continuous/integer problems, which are common in practice.

strengths: The paper tackles a genuine and underexplored gap: most ML-based MILP heuristics only handle binary variables and delegate a sub-problem to a traditional solver, whereas this work attempts a fully learned solver for integer variables.

The two-phase reward design (feasibility-seeking phase1, improvement-seeking phase2) is a reasonably principled way to decompose the MILP solving process for an RL agent, and Proposition 1 gives a simple theoretical justification for biasing the search between the LP-relaxation bound and the current incumbent.
The architecture (MPNN + Transformer encoder + periodic embeddings + phase token) is described in detail, and ablations (Table 3) isolate the contribution of each component reasonably well.

Reasonable reproducibility effort: pseudocode for training and search (Algorithms 1-2), explicit hyperparameters, dataset generation procedure, and hardware/software details are provided in the appendix.
weaknesses: Severe scale mismatch with the paper's own motivation: the introduction argues integer variables and real-world scale matter (logistics, energy systems), yet the largest tested instance is only 300 variables x 100 constraints, which Gurobi solves to optimality in under 1 second. This undermines the practical significance of the contribution and leaves open whether the method has any advantage at scales where traditional solvers actually struggle.

The comparison to Gurobi is close to vacuous: since BKS is essentially Gurobi's exact solution and Gurobi solves every instance in <1s with 0% (or near-0%) gap, the reported 'near-optimal' results for RL-MILP (taking up to 100s and still leaving 0.3-0.65% gaps) do not demonstrate any practical benefit over simply calling Gurobi. No argument or evidence is given for scenarios where this trade-off would be favorable (e.g., harder instances, repeated similar instances, or solver-unavailable settings).

Missing comparisons to actual state-of-the-art baselines from the literature (e.g., Gasse et al. 2019, Nair et al. 2020, Han et al. 2023 predict-and-search, or the Feasibility Pump that is explicitly discussed in the preliminaries). The chosen baselines (M_MLP, M_CNN) are ad hoc variants created solely by swapping the Transformer encoder, effectively duplicating the ablation study rather than benchmarking against established competing methods.

The 'full end-to-end, no traditional solver' claim is not fully substantiated: the method still appears to rely on solving the LP relaxation to obtain objr for the reward signal and search guidance (Algorithm 1, line 3, 'Relaxation(M)'), which itself typically requires a solver, creating tension with the claimed independence from off-the-shelf solvers.

Generalization across problem sizes/structures is not demonstrated -- the model appears to be trained and evaluated separately per fixed (n, m) dataset, with no experiment showing transfer to unseen sizes, sparsity patterns, or realistic MILP benchmark families (e.g., set covering, facility location, combinatorial auctions) commonly used in the ML4CO literature, limiting confidence in the method's general usefulness.

The synthetic data generation (Table 4) is simplistic (uniform random coefficients, fixed density) and not tied to any realistic MILP application despite the paper's motivating examples (logistics, maritime transport, energy systems); no real-world or standard benchmark instances are tested.

No wall-clock/scalability analysis of training cost or inference cost as problem size grows, and no discussion of how training time or sample complexity scales with n and m, which is critical for an RL-based approach intended to generalize beyond toy sizes.

Proposition 1 is a fairly straightforward restatement of the standard LP-relaxation bounding argument used in branch-and-bound (i.e., objr is a valid lower bound and any improving solution must lie between the bound and incumbent), so its 'theoretical foundation' framing somewhat overstates the novelty of this contribution.

strengths: Addresses an underexplored aspect of ML-for-MILP: handling non-binary integer variables directly rather than only binary variables, which is a reasonable and timely motivation.

The paper provides a theoretical justification (Proposition 1, with proof in the appendix) linking the LP-relaxation bound and current best solution to guide the reward design, giving the method a principled foundation rather than being purely heuristic.

The two-phase reward design (feasibility-seeking phase1, improvement-seeking phase2) and the toward-optimal bias parameter β are clearly motivated and empirically analyzed (Table 1, Figure 6/7), showing the intended effect on solution quality.

Reasonably thorough ablation study (Table 3) isolating the contributions of the Transformer encoder, MPNN, periodic embedding, separated layers, and phase token, and a separate study on neighborhood/action-set size (Table 2).

Good reproducibility support: detailed pseudocode for the learning algorithm and search strategy (Appendices C, D), dataset generation parameters, hardware/software environment, and hyperparameters (Appendix E).

The Transformer-based GNN architecture to mitigate MPNN oversmoothing and capture long-range variable-constraint relationships is a sensible architectural choice motivated by the bipartite graph diameter issue illustrated in Figure 2.
weaknesses: Significance is undermined by the experimental results themselves: Gurobi solves all tested instances (up to D300x100) to near-optimality in under 1 second, while RL-MILP consistently has a worse Gap than Gurobi across every dataset and β setting in Table 1. Since the exact solver is both faster and more accurate on these benchmarks, the practical motivation for the proposed method is unclear — the paper does not test on instances large/hard enough that Gurobi would actually struggle, which is where a learning-based full end-to-end solver would matter.

The most directly relevant baseline, Qi et al. (2021) "Smart Feasibility Pump," an RL-based MILP method discussed at length in the introduction and related work as the closest prior work, is never included in the experimental comparison (Table 1/2/3). Excluding it leaves the central claim of improvement over prior RL-based feasibility-pump approaches empirically unsupported.

Despite being framed as a solver for "Mixed-Integer Linear Programs," the experiments only cover pure integer programs (all variables integer); no results are shown for genuinely mixed continuous/integer instances, which somewhat overstates the generality implied by the title and abstract.

All experiments use synthetically generated instances from a single narrow generator (Qi et al. 2021 style, uniform random coefficients), with no evaluation on standard/real-world benchmark libraries (e.g., MIPLIB) or more heterogeneous constraint structures, limiting confidence in generalizability.

The comparison baselines M_MLP and M_CNN are ad hoc architecture substitutions rather than established published methods, and the LS baseline is a simplified local search starting from the RL agent's own feasible point, which may somewhat favor the proposed method's narrative; a stronger set of published end-to-end/primal-heuristic baselines (adapted where possible) would strengthen the evidentiary basis.

Training cost/time for the RL agent is not reported, and it is unclear whether a single trained agent generalizes across instance sizes/distributions or a new agent must be retrained per dataset size, which matters for the claimed scalability and practicality of the approach.

strengths: Addresses a genuine gap in the literature: existing end-to-end learning primal heuristics (E2EPH) typically rely on an ILP solver to repair infeasible ML predictions and are largely restricted to binary variables; RL-SPH removes the solver dependency and explicitly targets general (non-binary) integer variables, which are common in practice but underexplored in this line of work.

The proposed RL framework is carefully designed for ILP structure: a two-phase reward (feasibility-seeking then optimization-seeking), a Transformer-based GNN to capture long-range variable-constraint dependencies beyond what shallow MPNNs can model, and a neighborhood-based variable selection strategy inspired by local search/RENS/LNS.

Comprehensive empirical comparison against four standard start primal heuristics (Diving, FP, Rounding, RENS) and against SCIP/PAS combined with an ILP solver, showing consistent and often large improvements in feasibility rate, primal gap, and primal integral.

Reasonably thorough ablation study isolating the contribution of the transformer encoder, reward context, and phase-separated layers, showing each component matters (e.g., without the transformer encoder the model fails to find any feasible solution on CA).
Good reproducibility effort: detailed appendices specifying dataset generation parameters, hyperparameters, training times, hardware, and pseudocode for the RL loop and variable-selection procedure.
weaknesses: The central theoretical claim (Proposition 1) is much weaker than the paper's framing suggests. It merely shows that IF Rt,bound=0 and Rt,const>0 hold for all t<T (i.e., if the sequence of constraint violations is assumed to monotonically improve while bounds are always respected), THEN the solution becomes feasible by a telescoping-sum argument — this is close to a restatement of the reward definition rather than a guarantee that a trained policy will actually satisfy these conditions. The abstract/conclusion's language of 'theoretically guaranteeing feasibility' overstates what is proven; no argument is given for why a learned policy would satisfy the proposition's antecedent in general.

Evaluation coverage in the solver-combination experiment (Section 4.3, Table 2) is limited to only IS and NBI, omitting CA, SC, and MVC that were used in the first experiment, which weakens the generality of the 'RL-SPH+solver beats SCIP/PAS' claim. Likewise, the ablation study (Table 3) only covers IS and CA, not all five benchmarks.

All benchmarks are synthetically generated (Barabási–Albert graphs, randomly generated coefficients), with no evaluation on real-world or standard MIP benchmark libraries (e.g., MIPLIB), leaving open how the method performs on realistic, more heterogeneous instances.

Training is per-benchmark and apparently per-instance-size/distribution (with training times up to 83 minutes for MVC), and there is no experiment testing generalization to different instance sizes, densities, or distributions than those trained on, which is an important practical consideration for a method intended as a general-purpose primal heuristic.

The comparison protocol for start primal heuristics (Section 4.1.2) disables SCIP's presolving and branching for the baselines to "isolate heuristic performance," which could handicap the baselines relative to their typical use inside a full solver, and RL-SPH's own stopping condition (running until baselines finish) is not a clearly matched or standard time-limited comparison, making runtime/quality trade-offs harder to interpret.

The mechanism for fixing variables in RL-SPH+SCIP based on an ensemble of feasible solutions from the first 5 seconds is described only briefly ('unanimous value'), lacking detail on how many candidate solutions are pooled, how ties or partial agreement are handled, and how sensitive results are to this design choice.

Scalability of the Transformer-based GNN (quadratic attention cost) to substantially larger instances than tested (up to ~4000 variables) is not discussed or empirically examined, raising questions about applicability to larger real-world ILPs.

strengths: Addresses a genuine gap in the E2EPH literature: prior learning-based primal heuristics rely on an ILP solver to repair infeasibility and mostly handle only binary variables, whereas RL-SPH targets independent feasibility restoration and explicitly supports general (non-binary) integer variables.

The RL formulation is carefully designed: a two-phase reward (feasibility-seeking then optimization-seeking), an exploration penalty, and a toward-optimal bias, together with an accompanying (albeit idealized) monotonicity argument (Proposition 1) motivating why the agent should discover feasibility.

The architectural choice of a Transformer-based GNN to overcome oversmoothing/limited receptive field of standard MPNN-based bipartite-graph encoders used in prior work is well-motivated with a concrete example (Figure 2a) showing why long-range dependencies matter for ILP.

Reasonably broad empirical study: comparisons against four classical SCIP start heuristics, against an existing E2EPH+solver baseline (PAS+SCIP), and an ablation over three architectural components (reward context, phase-separated layers, transformer encoder), with reported feasibility rate, primal gap, and primal integral.
The paper is generally well organized, with an explicit problem formulation, algorithmic pseudocode, and appendix derivations that aid reproducibility of the reward/search logic.
weaknesses: Timing/compute comparisons appear potentially unfair: RL-SPH has no predefined termination and is allowed to run until all baselines finish, while it also required substantial per-dataset training time (23–83 minutes, Table 6) that is not obviously amortized or accounted for in the primal-integral comparisons against classical (training-free) SCIP heuristics; it's unclear how inference wall-clock time (GPU vs CPU, model overhead per step) is normalized between RL-SPH and Diving/FP/Rounding/RENS.

The theoretical 'guarantee' of feasibility (Proposition 1) is conditioned on assumptions (Rt,const>0 and Rt,bound=0 for all t<T) that are not shown to actually hold for the trained policy; it is essentially a property of the reward telescoping sum rather than a proof that the learned agent will satisfy these preconditions, so calling it a theoretical guarantee of feasibility is somewhat overstated.

Evaluation coverage is inconsistent across experiments: the solver-combination experiment (Table 2) is run on only 2 of the 5 benchmarks (IS, NBI), and the ablation study (Table 3) is run on only 2 benchmarks (IS, CA), limiting confidence that the reported gains generalize across all problem classes introduced earlier (SC, MVC, CA are dropped in later experiments without explanation).

Comparisons to recent, directly relevant E2EPH baselines cited in Related Work (Huang et al. 2024 Contrastive P&S, Liu et al. 2025 Apollo-MILP) are absent; only the older PAS (2023) baseline is used, weakening the claim that RL-SPH advances the state of the art among learning-based methods.

RL-SPH requires training a dedicated agent per problem distribution/size (tens of minutes to over an hour), which is a substantial practical limitation for a 'primal heuristic' whose classical appeal is being training-free and instantly deployable to new instances/problem types; this trade-off is not discussed as a limitation.

High variance is observed in several primal-gap results (e.g., CA PG 3.82±9.77, SC PG 9.67±15.41), and PG/PI are averaged only over instances with at least one feasible solution, which can bias comparisons across methods with very different feasibility rates (e.g., Diving's 0% PG on SC is based on only 1% FR, essentially a degenerate comparison that is not clearly flagged as such in the main text).

The discrete action space (±1 change per variable per step) seems ill-suited to non-binary integer variables with wide bounds; no analysis is given of how many timesteps/actions are needed to correct large deviations, nor of scalability as variable ranges grow, which is central to the paper's claimed contribution on non-binary integers.

No code or artifact release is mentioned, and several implementation choices (e.g., initial random-assignment heuristic details, hyperparameter sensitivity beyond alpha) rely on appendix descriptions rather than releasable code, which somewhat limits practical reproducibility despite detailed textual descriptions.

strengths: Clear, well-motivated problem framing: RL-SPH is (to the authors' knowledge) the first end-to-end learned primal heuristic that can independently produce feasible ILP solutions, including for non-binary integer variables with unbounded domains, which prior E2EPH approaches (relying on ILP solvers or fixed bit-width binary encodings) cannot handle.

The paper provides a formal feasibility guarantee (Proposition 1) tied directly to the reward design, giving the method a principled foundation beyond pure empiricism; the proof is included and appears correct given the stated assumptions.

The architecture choices are well justified: a Transformer-based GNN is motivated by a concrete argument about long-range variable dependencies and oversmoothing in shallow MPNNs, and Periodic Embeddings are used to sensibly handle unbounded integer values.

Experiments span five diverse NP-hard benchmarks (IS, CA, SC, MVC, NBI) and report multiple metrics (FR, PG, PI) with variance, showing consistent and often large improvements over standard start heuristics (Diving, FP, Rounding, RENS) and a representative E2EPH baseline (PAS) combined with SCIP.

The paper includes a thorough appendix with full training procedure, hyperparameters, dataset generation details, an ablation study on GNN components, and additional analysis of the toward-optimal bias parameter, supporting reproducibility.
The limitations of reduced problem size (potential sub-optimality) are honestly acknowledged rather than hidden.
weaknesses: The solver-integration comparison (Section 4.3) only includes SCIP and a single, relatively older E2EPH baseline (PAS, 2023); more recent trust-region/contrastive-search methods discussed in Related Work (Huang et al. 2024, Liu et al. 2025) are not empirically compared, despite being cited as the closest competing approaches, leaving the practical advantage over current SOTA less clear.

The GNN ablation study (Table 3) is conducted on only two of the five benchmarks (IS and CA), limiting confidence that the conclusions about component importance generalize across problem types (especially non-binary integer instances).

The PAS+S vs RL-SPH+S comparison is effectively only apples-to-apples on IS, since PAS does not support the NBI benchmark; this restricts the strength of the claim that RL-SPH is uniformly superior when combined with a solver.

Reward function design (Eqs. 6-8) is fairly intricate and heuristic in the optimization phase, with several manually chosen cases and a tunable bias parameter α; while ablated in the appendix, the design lacks the same theoretical justification given to the feasibility guarantee.

Action magnitude is fixed to unit increments per step, which may require many timesteps to reach far-off optimal integer values for variables with large ranges; scalability of the approach to larger instances or variables with very wide domains is not directly studied.

Only 100 test instances per benchmark and a single synthetic NBI benchmark are used; broader validation on real-world integer-variable ILPs (e.g., logistics, energy systems mentioned in the intro) is missing, so the practical significance of the integer-variable contribution is only partially demonstrated.

Training time (23–83 minutes per dataset) is reported but not integrated into an end-to-end wall-clock comparison against baseline solving times, making it harder to assess the true total-cost trade-off of the learning-based approach in practice.

strengths: Addresses a genuinely underexplored and important problem: independently generating feasible ILP solutions via ML without relying on an external solver, including for non-binary integer variables, which most prior E2EPH work has not tackled.

Very extensive empirical evaluation: five benchmark families, comparisons against four SPH baselines and three SOTA E2EPH methods, ablations on the search strategy and architecture, cross-problem generalization, robustness to distribution/size/density shifts, MIPLIB generalization tests, and solver-integration experiments (SCIP and Gurobi).

The two-phase reward design and feasibility-aware variable selection are intuitive and well-motivated, and the ablation studies (Tables 5-6) convincingly show each component's contribution to feasibility and solution quality.

Training efficiency is a real practical advantage: RL-SPH needs no near-optimal solution labels and trains an order of magnitude faster than compared supervised/unsupervised E2EPH baselines, while using one consistent hyperparameter configuration across all datasets.
Reasonably transparent reporting of limitations and negative/mixed results (e.g., NBI PG worse than RHF, MVC training taking much longer, scalability concerns candidly discussed in the appendix).
weaknesses: The theoretical result (Proposition 1) assumes idealized per-step conditions (Rt,const>0 and Rt,bound=0 for all t<T) that essentially presuppose good agent behavior; the empirical "adherence rate" is only 88-99%, meaning the formal guarantee does not actually hold for the trained policy, so the claimed "theoretical reward-feasibility alignment" is weaker than the framing suggests.

The claim of being "first to establish reward-feasibility alignment" and achieving 100% FR is somewhat overstated in the abstract/intro, since a simple classical baseline (RHF) also attains 100% FR across all benchmarks in the main experiments; the paper's real advantage lies mainly in solution quality (PG/PI) at equal feasibility, which is a more modest but still useful claim.

Superiority is not fully consistent: on NBI, RHF achieves a strictly better PG (0.00%) than RL-SPH(LP) (0.22%), and RL-SPH(Random) underperforms substantially on NBI PG (28.32%), undercutting the claimed uniform dominance over baselines.

The method restricts variable updates to unit magnitude (Δx=1) by design; while the appendix shows larger step sizes improve quality, the main results use the more limited setting, which caps how close RL-SPH gets to optimality and is acknowledged only as future work.

Computational complexity of the variable-selection step is O(mn) and could become a bottleneck as m≈n grows large (self-acknowledged in Appendix I.5); no experiments are shown on very large-scale ILPs (beyond ~10,000 variables) to validate the scalability claims made about real-world logistics/maritime applications.

The comparison protocol (RL-SPH runs until baselines complete their search, with no predefined termination) introduces some ambiguity in how time budgets are equalized across very different heuristics, and different time limits are used across benchmarks (e.g., 30s for IS vs 1000s elsewhere), which could affect the fairness of cross-method comparisons.

strengths: Addresses a genuine gap: existing end-to-end learning primal heuristics (E2EPH) typically cannot guarantee feasibility and depend on external solvers; the paper targets this directly with a start primal heuristic (SPH) that works without a solver in the loop.
Extends beyond binary variables to non-binary integers (NBI benchmark), which most prior E2EPH work ignores.

Extensive empirical evaluation: five benchmarks, four SPH baseline families and three E2EPH baselines, cross-problem generalization, MIPLIB tests, distribution/size/density shift experiments, solver integration (SCIP/Gurobi), and multiple ablations (search strategy, architecture components, hyperparameters).

Reasonably efficient training relative to supervised/unsupervised E2EPH baselines (tens of minutes vs. hours), and uses a single hyperparameter configuration across datasets, which is a practical advantage if genuinely as robust as claimed.
Design choices (two-phase reward, feasibility-aware neighbor selection, periodic embeddings for unbounded integers) are reasonably well-motivated and ablated.
weaknesses: The central theoretical contribution (Proposition 1) is close to circular: it assumes exactly the idealized behavior needed for feasibility (Rt,const>0 and Rt,bound=0 for all t<T) as a hypothesis and then shows this behavior leads to feasibility. This is a sanity-check-style derivation, not evidence that a trained policy will actually satisfy these conditions; the paper's own Table 3 shows adherence rates as low as 88.4% (NBI) and 91.5% (CA), undermining the strength of the 'theoretically established reward-feasibility alignment' claim repeated throughout the abstract/intro/conclusion.

Despite the headline '28.6x lower primal gap' claim, RL-SPH is not uniformly better than the strongest classical baseline (RHF): on NBI, RL-SPH has a *higher* PG than RHF (0.22 vs 0.00), and on SC, RL-SPH's PG (9.67±15.41) is worse than RHF's, with very large variances across several settings (e.g., CA PG 3.82±9.77, SC 9.67±15.41), suggesting inconsistent and sometimes unreliable performance rather than a clean dominance story.

Evaluation protocol is inconsistent across experiments: time limits vary arbitrarily (30s, 50s, 150s, 300s, 1000s) across different tables without clear justification, and RL-SPH is allowed to run until baselines finish rather than under a fixed shared budget, complicating fair comparison.

The comparison omits a crucial practical dimension: classical SPH baselines (DHF, FP, RHF, RENS) require no training at all, whereas RL-SPH requires ~30–90 minutes of instance-distribution-specific training; this asymmetry is not incorporated into the headline metrics (PG/PI/FT), potentially overstating practical speed advantages.

Baseline treatment may be uneven: SCIP heuristics are run with presolving/branching disabled 'to isolate heuristic performance,' which could handicap classical methods relative to how they'd perform in practice, while E2EPH baselines were given benchmark-specific tuning (framed as unfair to them) but also trained on instance sizes that may not match their original settings (e.g., CA/SC sizes differ substantially from DiffILO's original benchmarks), raising the possibility that reported E2EPH failures partly reflect this mismatch rather than a fundamental limitation.

Feasibility rate (FR) is elevated as the 'primary metric' in a way that appears to favor the proposed method, since RL-SPH is specifically engineered around achieving feasibility (via its reward and search design) — a somewhat self-serving framing given that solution quality (PG) is often mediocre or worse relative to the strongest 100%-FR baseline.

Generalization beyond training distribution is limited: cross-problem generalization requires joint training on both problem types (fails when trained on only one), and MIPLIB results show degraded/unstable performance on instances that differ substantially in scale (e.g., scpk4) or constraint type (e.g., Set Partitioning in bppc8-02), indicating limited transfer beyond narrowly matched settings.

The approach still fixes movement magnitude to 1 by design choice to 'prioritize feasibility over optimality,' and the appendix shows this materially limits solution quality (Table 22); this restricts real-world applicability since actual downstream optimality (not just feasibility) is the ultimate goal.

Originality is somewhat incremental: the work combines known ingredients (actor-critic RL, Graph Transformer for long-range dependencies, RENS/LNS-style neighborhood search, periodic embeddings) rather than introducing fundamentally new algorithmic or architectural ideas; the main novelty is the specific reward decomposition and search strategy tailored to ILP feasibility.

strengths: Addresses a genuine and underexplored gap: prior end-to-end learning-based primal heuristics rely on external ILP solvers to achieve feasibility, whereas RL-SPH is explicitly designed to produce feasible ILP solutions independently, including for non-binary integer variables, which most prior E2EPH work ignores.

The paper provides an unusually extensive empirical evaluation: comparisons against four classical SPH baseline families and three SOTA E2EPH methods across five benchmarks, plus cross-problem generalization, distribution-shift, size-shift, density-shift experiments, MIPLIB evaluation on 17 diverse unseen instances, solver-integration experiments (SCIP and Gurobi), and multiple ablations (search strategy, ILP-GT architecture components, toward-optimal bias, neighbor ratio).

A theoretical proposition (reward-feasibility alignment) is provided and empirically validated via adherence-rate measurements (88-99% across datasets), giving some principled grounding to the reward design rather than relying purely on empirical tuning.

Reports strong, consistent 100% feasibility rate across all tested benchmarks with a single fixed hyperparameter configuration (unlike baselines that require per-dataset tuning), and demonstrates substantially lower training cost (30 min average) compared to supervised/unsupervised E2EPH baselines.
The ILP-GT architecture is reasonably motivated (addressing oversmoothing/long-range dependency limitations of MPNNs used in prior work) and supported by a qualitative attention-distance case study.

Honest and fairly extensive limitations/future-work discussion (Appendix I), including scalability bottlenecks, nonlinear constraint applicability, and directions to improve optimality, which strengthens the credibility of the claims.
weaknesses: Proposition 1 is a fairly weak theoretical result: it assumes Rt,const > 0 and Rt,bound = 0 hold for all t < T (i.e., assumes the exact behavior the RL agent is supposed to learn), so the proof is nearly tautological and does not establish that a trained policy will actually satisfy these conditions; the paper only supports this via an empirical adherence rate (as low as 88.4% on NBI), leaving a nontrivial gap between theory and practice that is not fully reconciled.

Performance is uneven in places despite the strong headline claims: e.g., RL-SPH(LP) has a notably worse PG than RHF on NBI (0.22 vs 0.00) and RL-SPH(Random) performs far worse on NBI (28.32% PG), and first-feasible-solution time is sometimes worse than RHF (e.g., IS: 0.55s vs 0.10s, MVC: 1.55s vs 0.20s), so the reported aggregate improvements partly mask per-dataset weaknesses.

Scalability is a real concern: the method's complexity is O(mn + ñ²) per step, and the MIPLIB experiment shows a clear degradation on the largest instance (scpk4, 100k variables) where RL-SPH performs much worse than RHF, suggesting the approach may not scale gracefully to industrial-scale ILPs without further engineering (acknowledged only briefly in the appendix).

The reward function design (Eqs. 4-8) is intricate with many hand-crafted cases, scaling factors, and phase-dependent branches, which raises reproducibility and generalizability concerns beyond the five curated synthetic benchmark families, even though hyperparameters are kept fixed.

Benchmarks are largely synthetic (Barabasi-Albert/Erdos-Renyi generated instances) rather than real-world industrial ILPs; the MIPLIB generalization results, while a nice addition, are limited to instances that RL-SPH was never trained to handle structurally (e.g., set-partitioning constraints), and results there are mixed.

The comparison baselines for E2EPH (PAS, DDIM, DiffILO) are evaluated on only three of the five benchmarks (SC, CA, IS), and PAS is excluded from SC due to lack of provided hyperparameters, somewhat limiting the completeness of the head-to-head SOTA comparison.
